title: A Voice Memo About the Man Who Cut the Line
script: Narrator: [tired] Voice memo to myself, Tuesday evening. I want to remember what happened today at the pharmacy, because I am still thinking about it.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I was waiting in line for almost twenty minutes, because the pharmacist was slow and there were many customers before me.
Narrator: [annoyed] Then a man walked straight to the front and started talking to the pharmacist, as if the line did not exist at all.
Narrator: [honestly] My first feeling was anger. I wanted to shout at him, because I had been standing there so patiently.
Narrator: [reflective] But before I said anything, an older woman behind me spoke calmly. She said, excuse me sir, we have all been waiting, so please join the line.
Narrator: [surprised] The man looked embarrassed. He apologized quietly and walked to the back of the line without arguing further.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I was impressed, because the woman did not shout or insult him. She simply reminded him of what was fair, in a calm and steady voice.
Narrator: [reflective] Later, while I was walking home, I thought about how she handled it, and I realized something important about adab.
Narrator: [warmly] Adab is not only about staying silent when someone is wrong. Sometimes real respect means speaking up, but doing it calmly and kindly.
Narrator: [honestly] If I had shouted instead, the situation would have become worse, and everyone in the pharmacy would have felt uncomfortable and tense.
Narrator: [determined] Next time something like this happens, I want to remember her voice, calm but firm, not angry and not silent either.
Narrator: [gently] I think good manners are sometimes braver than staying quiet, because you have to care enough to say something, while staying kind while doing it.
Narrator: [warmly] So that is my note to myself tonight. Speak calmly, even when you feel frustrated, because how you say something matters just as much as what you say.
Narrator: [peacefully] I hope, next time I am the one who is wrong, someone corrects me with the same patience that woman showed today.

quiz.question: Why was the narrator waiting so long at the pharmacy?
options: The pharmacist was slow and there were many customers
She was chatting with a friend
quiz.explanation: She says she waited almost twenty minutes because the pharmacist was slow and many customers were ahead of her.

quiz.question: What did the man do that upset the narrator?
options: He walked to the front of the line as if it did not exist
He talked loudly on the phone
quiz.explanation: The man walked straight to the front and spoke to the pharmacist, ignoring the line.

quiz.question: What did the older woman say to the man?
options: She asked him to join the line since everyone had been waiting
quiz.explanation: The woman calmly told him everyone had been waiting and asked him to join the line.

quiz.question: How did the man react to the woman's words?
options: He looked embarrassed and went to the back of the line
quiz.explanation: He looked embarrassed, apologized quietly, and walked to the back of the line without arguing.

quiz.question: What lesson does the narrator take from this moment?
options: Speak up calmly and kindly instead of shouting or staying silent
Shouting is the best way to fix problems
quiz.explanation: She concludes that real respect sometimes means speaking up, but doing it calmly, rather than shouting or staying silent.

title: Bima Calls to Apologize for Interrupting in the Meeting
script: Bima: [nervous] Laras, do you have a minute? I wanted to call you about the meeting this afternoon.
Laras: [calmly] Of course, Bima. What's on your mind?
Bima: [regretfully] I interrupted you twice while you were presenting the budget report, and I have felt bad about it since then.
Laras: [thoughtful] I noticed that too, actually. What happened?
Bima: [honestly] I was excited about my idea, so I spoke before you finished your sentence, both times. I did not mean to be disrespectful.
Laras: [gently] I understand that excitement can make us forget our manners sometimes, but it did make me lose my train of thought.
Bima: [softly] I know interrupting someone who is speaking shows a lack of respect, even when the intention behind it is good.
Laras: [warmly] I appreciate that you noticed and called me about it afterward. That says a lot about you as a colleague.
Bima: [thoughtful] I keep thinking about how it must have looked to the rest of the team, as if I did not value your presentation.
Laras: [kindly] Honestly, nobody else seemed to notice as much as you think they did. But I am glad you are aware of it.
Bima: [determined] Next time I have an idea during a meeting, I will write it down and wait until you finish speaking completely.
Laras: [encouraging] That's a smart habit. You can also just raise your hand quietly if the idea feels urgent to share.
Bima: [relieved] Thank you for not being upset with me. I really respect you as a colleague and as a friend.
Laras: [warmly] I am not upset at all. Everyone learns these things eventually, so please do not worry too much about it.
Bima: [warmly] Still, I wanted to apologize properly, instead of just saying a quick sorry tomorrow morning before the next meeting.
Laras: [touched] I appreciate that more than you know, Bima. Thank you for calling and being honest with me.
Bima: [smiling] Of course. See you at tomorrow's meeting, and I promise to listen more carefully this time.
Laras: [smiling] I look forward to it. Have a good evening, Bima, and thank you again for this call.

quiz.question: Why is Bima calling Laras?
options: To apologize for interrupting her during a meeting
To share a new project idea
quiz.explanation: Bima calls to apologize for interrupting Laras twice while she was presenting the budget report.

quiz.question: Why did Bima interrupt Laras during the presentation?
options: He wanted to end the meeting early
He was excited about his idea and spoke before she finished
He was asked to by another coworker
quiz.explanation: Bima explains he was excited about his idea, so he spoke before she finished her sentence.

quiz.question: How does Laras respond to Bima's apology?
options: She says she is very upset with him
She appreciates that he noticed and called her about it
She refuses to speak with him
She ends the meeting for tomorrow
quiz.explanation: Laras tells Bima she appreciates that he noticed and called her, saying it says a lot about him.

quiz.question: What does Bima plan to do next time he has an idea in a meeting?
options: Interrupt again if it feels important
Write it down and wait until Laras finishes speaking
Send her a message instead of attending
Ask someone else to speak for him
quiz.explanation: Bima decides to write his idea down and wait until Laras finishes speaking completely.

quiz.question: What does Laras suggest as an alternative if an idea feels urgent?
quiz.explanation: Laras suggests Bima could raise his hand quietly if the idea feels urgent to share.

title: A Radio Segment on Staying Polite Behind the Wheel
script: Radio Host: [cheerfully] Good afternoon, listeners! Today we are talking about adab on the road, because traffic can bring out the worst in people. We have a caller on the line.
Caller: [a little nervous] Hello! Thank you for taking my call this afternoon.
Radio Host: [warmly] Of course! What made you want to talk about this topic today?
Caller: [thoughtful] Well, I used to get very angry while driving, honking my horn whenever someone was slow or made a small mistake.
Radio Host: [curious] What changed for you?
Caller: [reflective] One day, I honked loudly at a car in front of me, although the driver was clearly an elderly man who looked nervous.
Radio Host: [interested] What happened after that moment?
Caller: [softly] When I finally passed him, I saw his face. He looked frightened, not annoyed, and I felt terrible almost immediately.
Radio Host: [gently] That sounds like a powerful moment to experience.
Caller: [honestly] It was. I realized I had been treating strangers on the road like they did not matter, just because I could not see their faces closely.
Radio Host: [curious] So what do you do differently now, when someone drives slowly in front of you?
Caller: [warmly] Now, before I honk, I ask myself if it is truly necessary, or if I am simply feeling impatient.
Radio Host: [interested] Do you have any other habits you changed since then?
Caller: [gently] Yes, I always let pedestrians cross first, even when I am in a hurry, because their safety matters more than my few extra seconds.
Radio Host: [curious] What would you say to listeners who feel frustrated in traffic every single day?
Caller: [encouraging] I would say, remember that every car has a person inside, someone's parent or someone's child, so treat them the way you would want to be treated.
Radio Host: [smiling] That's such an important reminder for all of us. Thank you so much for calling in today.
Caller: [warmly] Thank you for listening. I hope someone drives a little more gently after hearing this conversation.

quiz.question: What is today's radio segment about?
options: Adab on the road while driving
quiz.explanation: The host introduces today's topic as adab on the road, since traffic can bring out the worst in people.

quiz.question: How did the caller used to behave while driving?
options: She honked her horn whenever someone was slow or made a mistake
quiz.explanation: She admits she used to get angry and honk whenever someone was slow or made a small mistake.

quiz.question: Who was the caller honking at when her feelings changed?
options: An elderly man who looked nervous
quiz.explanation: She honked at a car driven by a clearly elderly and nervous man.

quiz.question: What does the caller ask herself now before honking?
options: Whether it is truly necessary or she is just impatient
Whether other cars will honk too
quiz.explanation: She now asks herself if honking is truly necessary or if she is just feeling impatient.

quiz.question: What is the caller's main message to frustrated drivers?
options: Every car has a person inside, so treat them as you want to be treated
quiz.explanation: She reminds listeners that every car has a person inside and to treat them the way they would want to be treated.

title: The Wedding Where I Finally Learned to Listen
script: Narrator: [warmly] Last month, I went to my cousin's wedding, and something happened there that I still think about often.
Narrator: [thoughtful] During the dinner, I was sitting next to my great-uncle, a man who talks slowly and tells very long stories.
Narrator: [honestly] In the past, I usually found an excuse to leave when he started talking, because his stories felt endless and repetitive to me.
Narrator: [reflective] This time, my phone battery had died, so I could not escape into my phone like I normally would have.
Narrator: [gently] He began telling a story about how he met my great-aunt, sixty years ago, when they were both very young.
Narrator: [softly] At first, I listened only because I had no other choice, but slowly, the story began to pull me in completely.
Narrator: [warmly] He described the small letters they wrote to each other, and how nervous he felt the first time he visited her family.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I realized I had never actually asked him about his life before, even though he had been part of our family my whole life.
Narrator: [honestly] When he finished, he looked at me and said, thank you for listening, nobody has time for old stories anymore.
Narrator: [touched] That sentence hit me hard, because it was true. I had never given him my full attention before that night.
Narrator: [reflective] I understood then that listening is a form of adab too, maybe one of the quietest and most overlooked forms there is.
Narrator: [determined] Since that wedding, I try to sit with older relatives more often, and I leave my phone in my pocket when they speak.
Narrator: [warmly] It is a small change, but I think it means more to them than any gift I could ever buy.
Narrator: [peacefully] My great-uncle passed away a few weeks after that wedding, so I am grateful I finally listened, while there was still time.

quiz.question: Where does this story take place?
options: At a family dinner at home
quiz.explanation: The narrator says he went to his cousin's wedding last month.

quiz.question: Why couldn't the narrator escape into his phone this time?
options: He forgot his phone at home
His great-uncle asked him to put it away
He had no signal at the venue
quiz.explanation: He explains that his phone battery had died, so he could not escape into it like usual.

quiz.question: What story did the great-uncle tell?
options: How he met the narrator's great-aunt sixty years ago
A story about the wedding venue
A story about his childhood home
quiz.explanation: The great-uncle told the story of how he met the narrator's great-aunt sixty years ago.

quiz.question: What did the great-uncle say after finishing his story?
options: Thank you for listening, nobody has time for old stories anymore
That he wanted to leave early
quiz.explanation: He thanked the narrator for listening, saying nobody has time for old stories anymore.

quiz.question: What did the narrator start doing after this wedding?
options: Sitting with older relatives more and putting his phone away
Writing down family stories for a book
quiz.explanation: He began sitting with older relatives more often and leaving his phone in his pocket when they speak.

title: Two Coworkers Talk About Replying to Messages on Time
script: Citra: [curious] Reza, can I ask you something? Why do you always reply to messages so quickly, even late at night?
Reza: [smiling] Ha, it's a habit my old manager taught me. She said ignoring messages for days shows disrespect for the other person's time.
Citra: [thoughtful] I never really thought about it that way. I usually just reply whenever I feel like it.
Reza: [gently] I understand that, but imagine someone waiting for an answer because they need it to finish their own work.
Citra: [honestly] That's true. Last week, I left a client waiting for three days because I completely forgot to check my messages.
Reza: [nodding] That happens to everyone sometimes, but I try to at least send a short reply, even if I cannot answer fully yet.
Citra: [curious] What do you usually write when you are too busy to answer properly?
Reza: [warmly] Something simple, like, thank you for your message, I will answer properly by tomorrow. It only takes ten seconds to type.
Citra: [surprised] I never thought a quick reply like that could matter so much to someone.
Reza: [thoughtful] It does, because silence makes people feel ignored, even if you did not mean to ignore them at all.
Citra: [curious] Do you also have rules about how you write your replies to people?
Reza: [gently] Yes, actually. I always read the message twice before answering, so I do not misunderstand what they need from me.
Citra: [thoughtful] That's smart. I sometimes reply too fast and give the wrong answer, then I have to correct myself later.
Reza: [warmly] Exactly, so speed matters, but understanding matters even more. Adab in messages means being both prompt and thoughtful.
Citra: [smiling] I think I have been careless about this for a long time. I want to change that starting today.
Reza: [encouraging] Start small. Just answer within a day, even briefly, and people will notice the difference quickly.
Citra: [warmly] Thank you, Reza. I am going to reply to that client right now, even though it is three days late.
Reza: [laughing] Better late than never. Good luck with the reply!

quiz.question: Why is Citra curious about Reza's habit?
options: He always replies to messages quickly, even at night
He deletes messages without reading them
He asks others to reply for him
quiz.explanation: Citra asks why Reza always replies to messages so quickly, even late at night.

quiz.question: What did Reza's old manager teach him?
options: That ignoring messages for days shows disrespect for someone's time
To reply only once a week
To always call instead of texting
quiz.explanation: His manager told him ignoring messages for days shows disrespect for the other person's time.

quiz.question: What happened when Citra left a client waiting for three days?
options: She forgot to check her messages
quiz.explanation: Citra admits she left a client waiting for three days because she forgot to check her messages.

quiz.question: What does Reza suggest sending when he is too busy to reply fully?
options: A short message saying he will answer properly soon
quiz.explanation: He suggests a short reply like thanking them and saying he will answer properly by tomorrow.

quiz.question: What does Reza say matters even more than speed when replying?
options: Understanding what the person actually needs
quiz.explanation: Reza says speed matters, but understanding what someone needs matters even more.

title: What I Learned About Disagreeing Without Disrespect
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] For a long time, I believed that disagreeing with someone meant I had to prove them completely wrong.
Narrator: [honestly] When a friend or coworker said something I disagreed with, I would argue loudly until they gave up or simply walked away.
Narrator: [reflective] I thought winning the argument meant I had good ideas, but I never noticed how uncomfortable it made everyone around me.
Narrator: [gently] Then, a few months ago, a colleague disagreed with my plan during a meeting, but she did it so differently than I expected.
Narrator: [warmly] She said, I see your point, and I understand why you think that way, although I have a different idea I would like to share.
Narrator: [surprised] I was ready to defend myself immediately, but her calm words made me actually want to listen to her instead of arguing.
Narrator: [thoughtful] She explained her idea clearly, without raising her voice or making me feel foolish for having a different opinion.
Narrator: [reflective] By the end of the conversation, I even agreed that her plan was better, and I did not feel embarrassed at all.
Narrator: [honestly] I realized that my old way of arguing had won some debates, but it had also quietly damaged many friendships over the years.
Narrator: [determined] So now, when I disagree with someone, I try to start with something I genuinely respect about their idea first.
Narrator: [gently] Then I explain my different view calmly, using words like, I understand, but I see it a little differently than you.
Narrator: [warmly] This small change has made people more willing to actually consider my opinions, instead of simply defending themselves against me.
Narrator: [peacefully] I learned that adab in disagreement is not about staying silent, but about disagreeing without disrespecting the person standing in front of you.
Narrator: [with a small smile] Because you can be honest and kind at the same time, even when your opinions are completely different from each other.

quiz.question: What did the narrator used to believe about disagreeing?
options: That it should always be avoided
That she had to prove the other person completely wrong
That it was never worth doing
quiz.explanation: She believed disagreeing meant she had to prove the other person completely wrong.

quiz.question: How did her colleague disagree with her plan in the meeting?
options: By calmly acknowledging her point before sharing a different idea
By reporting it to a manager
quiz.explanation: The colleague calmly said she understood the narrator's point before sharing her own different idea.

quiz.question: How did the narrator react to her colleague's calm approach?
options: She actually wanted to listen instead of arguing
quiz.explanation: Her colleague's calm words made her actually want to listen instead of defending herself.

quiz.question: What does the narrator realize about her old way of arguing?
options: It had quietly damaged many friendships over the years
quiz.explanation: She realizes her old arguing style had quietly damaged many friendships over the years.

quiz.question: What does the narrator now do first when she disagrees with someone?
options: She starts with something she respects about their idea
She immediately states her own opinion
quiz.explanation: She now tries to start with something she genuinely respects about the other person's idea.

title: A Podcast on Adab When Visiting Your In-Laws
script: Host: [warmly] Welcome back to the show. Today my guest is Andi, who got married last year and wants to talk about visiting in-laws with proper adab. Thanks for joining me.
Andi: [pleasantly] Thank you for inviting me. This topic taught me a lot during my first year of marriage.
Host: [curious] What was the biggest lesson you learned about visiting your wife's parents?
Andi: [thoughtful] Honestly, I learned that small gestures matter more than big ones. Bringing a small gift every visit meant more to them than I expected.
Host: [interested] What kind of gifts do you usually bring when you visit?
Andi: [gently] Simple things, like fruit, or something my mother-in-law mentioned she needed. It shows I was actually listening during our last conversation.
Host: [curious] Did you struggle with anything when you first started visiting?
Andi: [honestly] Yes, sitting quietly while my father-in-law talked for a long time. I used to check my phone without realizing how rude it looked to him.
Host: [thoughtful] How did you fix that particular habit?
Andi: [warmly] My wife gently told me it bothered her father, so now I leave my phone in the car before we even arrive.
Host: [curious] What about disagreements? Do you ever disagree with your in-laws about something?
Andi: [reflective] Sometimes, but I learned to disagree gently, and only when it truly matters, because respect comes before being right.
Host: [interested] Any advice about helping around the house during your visits?
Andi: [gently] I always offer to help clean up after meals, even though my mother-in-law usually refuses. Offering shows I do not expect to be served like a guest.
Host: [curious] What would you tell someone about to meet their in-laws for the very first time?
Andi: [encouraging] I would say, listen more than you speak, arrive on time, and remember that patience shows more respect than clever words ever could.
Host: [smiling] Beautiful advice, Andi. Thank you so much for sharing your experience with us today.
Andi: [warmly] Thank you for having me. I hope it helps someone feel less nervous before their next family visit.

quiz.question: What is Andi's connection to the topic being discussed?
options: He got married last year and visits his wife's parents
quiz.explanation: Andi got married last year and shares his experience visiting his wife's parents.

quiz.question: What does Andi say matters more than expensive gifts?
options: Arriving late but with a big gift
Small gestures, like bringing something they mentioned needing
Sending a gift by mail instead
quiz.explanation: He explains that small gestures, like bringing something his mother-in-law mentioned needing, mean more than big ones.

quiz.question: What habit did Andi have to change regarding his phone?
options: He leaves it in the car before visiting his in-laws
He only uses it for photos
He gave his phone to his wife
quiz.explanation: He now leaves his phone in the car because checking it while his father-in-law spoke looked rude.

quiz.question: How does Andi handle disagreements with his in-laws?
options: He disagrees gently and only when it truly matters
He argues to prove his point
He asks his wife to disagree for him
quiz.explanation: He says he disagrees gently and only when it truly matters, because respect comes before being right.

quiz.question: What is Andi's main advice for someone meeting in-laws for the first time?
options: Speak as much as possible to seem confident
Listen more than you speak, arrive on time, and be patient
Bring the most expensive gift possible
quiz.explanation: Andi advises listening more than speaking, arriving on time, and showing patience as a sign of respect.
